Chased
CHAYST
v.t. (pret. & pp.)
From Old French chacier, to hunt or pursue, from Latin captare, to try to seize. Webster 1828: pursued; hunted; driven. In the covenant curses the terror of being chased is inflicted without any pursuer at all.

Biblical Definition

Leviticus 26 sets out what covenant unfaithfulness will cost, and the most frightening clause in it involves no army: I will send a faintness into their hearts in the lands of their enemies; and the sound of a shaken leaf shall chase them; and they shall flee, as fleeing from a sword; and they shall fall when none pursueth (Leviticus 26:36). God does not need to send a pursuer; He withdraws courage, and a falling leaf finishes the work. Moses states the arithmetic of the reverse case, where the chasing is Israel’s and the ratio is impossible: How should one chase a thousand, and two put ten thousand to flight, except their Rock had sold them, and the LORD had shut them up? (Deuteronomy 32:30). Victory and defeat alike are traced to the same hand. Bildad, wrong about Job but right about the wicked in general, describes the end: He shall be driven from light into darkness, and chased out of the world (Job 18:18). And Isaiah likens scattered Babylon to game: it shall be as the chased roe, and as a sheep that no man taketh up (Isaiah 13:14).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines CHASE as to pursue for the purpose of taking; to hunt; to drive away, to put to flight; hence CHASED, pursued, hunted, driven, put to flight.

expand to see more

CHASE, v.t. — To pursue for the purpose of taking, as game; to hunt.

To pursue, or drive, as a defeated enemy; to put to flight.

To drive away; to dispel; as, to chase away care.

CHASED, pp. — Pursued; sought; driven; dispelled; put to flight.

Old French chacier, from Latin captare, frequentative of capio, to take — the same root as catch and capture.

Key Scripture

Leviticus 26:36 — "And upon them that are left alive of you I will send a faintness into their hearts in the lands of their enemies; and the sound of a shaken leaf shall chase them; and they shall flee, as fleeing from a sword; and they shall fall when none pursueth."

Deuteronomy 32:30 — "How should one chase a thousand, and two put ten thousand to flight, except their Rock had sold them, and the LORD had shut them up?"

Job 18:18 — "He shall be driven from light into darkness, and chased out of the world."

Proverbs 28:1 — "The wicked flee when no man pursueth: but the righteous are bold as a lion."

Modern Corruption

Leviticus 26:36 and Proverbs 28:1 diagnose fear as a moral condition under God’s hand, which the therapeutic account of anxiety as a purely clinical event cannot supply.

expand to see more

Scripture is not indifferent to bodily affliction, and this dictionary does not deny that fear has physical causes or that lawful means may treat them. But Leviticus 26:36 describes a fear that is judicial: God sends a faintness of heart, and the sound of a leaf does the rest. Proverbs 28:1 states the same principle as a proverb — The wicked flee when no man pursueth — and pairs it with the boldness of the righteous. The modern therapeutic frame, which treats anxiety exclusively as a disorder to be managed and never as a condition that might be addressed by repentance and the fear of God, is not a neutral advance in knowledge; it is an anthropology, and it has quietly replaced a biblical one. Where guilt is the cause, only forgiveness is the cure, and no technique will reach it.

Deuteronomy 32:30 guards the doctrine of providence at its hardest point: defeat. Moses does not permit Israel to explain a rout by enemy strength or by tactical error. Except their Rock had sold them, and the LORD had shut them up — the cause is God’s judicial hand, and the same hand gives the impossible victories elsewhere in the book. This is the Reformed doctrine of providence extending to second causes and to evil suffered, without making God the author of sin. The 1689 Confession states it carefully: God ordains whatsoever comes to pass, yet so as the contingency of second causes is not taken away. A providence that governs only the pleasant half of history is not the providence of Scripture, and it will fail the believer exactly when he needs it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew radaph (H7291), to pursue or chase; nadad (H5074), to flee or wander; nus (H5127), to flee; Greek dioko (G1377), to pursue, to persecute.

expand to see more

Hebrew radaph (H7291) — to pursue, to chase; the sound of a shaken leaf shall chase them (Leviticus 26:36).

Hebrew nus (H5127) — to flee; they shall flee, as fleeing from a sword (Leviticus 26:36).

Hebrew nadad (H5074) — to wander or be chased away; used of the fugitive wicked (Job 18:18).

Greek dioko (G1377) — to pursue, and so to persecute; the New Testament counterpart of radaph.

Hebrew tsebi (H6643) — the roe or gazelle; as the chased roe (Isaiah 13:14).

Usage

"The sound of a shaken leaf shall chase them (Leviticus 26:36) — God withdraws courage, and a falling leaf finishes the work."

"Except their Rock had sold them (Deuteronomy 32:30) — defeat is traced to the same hand that gives victory."

"The wicked flee when no man pursueth (Proverbs 28:1) — guilt supplies its own pursuer."
